title: What Leaders Can Learn From Great Parents
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This essay draws a direct parallel between how skilled parents teach children responsibility and how leaders should develop accountability in team members. It identifies a four-step sequence from parenting research — assign a manageable task, accept a misstep will happen, allow natural consequences with empathy but no rescue, then reassign the same task — and argues leaders undermine growth the same way overprotective parents do, by shielding people from consequences or punishing mistakes too harshly instead of reassigning the task. The piece closes by noting the parallel is nearly exact: doing less, not more, is often what produces more responsible people.
points: Imports a four-step parenting framework for teaching responsibility (assign, allow misstep, allow consequences with empathy, reassign) directly into a leadership context.
Argues leaders sabotage accountability development the same way overprotective parents do — by interceding to prevent consequences.
Claims the most effective 'punishment' for a mistake is often simply the shared recognition that the ball was dropped, not a harsher penalty.
Frames reassigning the same task after a misstep as a critical trust signal that most team members rise to meet.
Closes with the counterintuitive claim that doing less — resisting the urge to run interference — produces more responsible people, for children and adults alike.
quotes: Extraordinary parents and parenting experts point to four critical steps for teaching children how to be responsible: Give the child a task or assignment they can handle. Accept that they are likely to misstep or misbehave. Express empathy, but allow them to live with the consequences of their misbehavior or error. Give them the same task again.
Children learn responsibility by making mistakes and then enduring the consequences before trying the same task again. Parents who step in and interrupt any step in the process inhibit learning.

Similarly to parents, good leaders learn to accept the mistakes team members make without a lot of concern or reaction. They know those mistakes are key to learning and critical for inculcating the value of accountability if they are tied to consequences.

Good leaders show their faith and confidence in team members by assigning them the same task or oversight again, even after a misstep. When given a chance to shine after a poor performance, most team members will rise to the occasion.
Too heavy a hand and people don’t become more responsible or accountable. They simply lose confidence. So much of leadership is doing less to achieve more.
